name: Transaction Throughput
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: How Many Transactions Can a Blockchain Actually Handle?
lesson.summary: Transaction throughput measures how many transactions a network can process in a given period, usually expressed in transactions per second, and it is the hard numeric ceiling that separates blockchains from the payment systems they hope to compete with.
lesson.body:
A transaction, as covered earlier, is a signed instruction that moves value or triggers a contract, and every transaction has to be included in a block before it counts as part of the ledger's history. Transaction throughput is simply the rate at which a network can absorb these transactions into blocks, typically measured in transactions per second (TPS). It sounds like a simple engineering number, but it is arguably the single statistic that most determines whether a blockchain can function as everyday payment infrastructure or remain a niche settlement system.

The numbers are more modest than most people expect. Bitcoin produces a block roughly every ten minutes, and each block has a fixed capacity, originally around one megabyte of transaction data, later effectively expanded by the SegWit upgrade. Given typical transaction sizes, this works out to somewhere around seven transactions per second on average. Ethereum, before its 2022 shift to proof of stake, processed transactions in the range of roughly fifteen to thirty per second, depending on how complex the transactions were. For comparison, Visa has publicly stated its network is engineered to handle tens of thousands of transactions per second at peak, though its actual average daily volume runs far lower than that peak figure. The gap between a blockchain's single-digit or low double-digit throughput and a card network's real-world capacity is the starting point for almost every serious critique of blockchain as a payments technology.

Why is the ceiling so low? Part of the answer connects directly to network latency. A block full of transactions has to physically propagate across a globally distributed set of nodes before the network can safely build the next block on top of it. If blocks were made much bigger, or produced much faster, propagation would take longer relative to the block interval, and nodes with slower connections would fall behind more often, increasing the odds that two miners produce competing blocks at nearly the same time. Protocol designers set block size and block interval as a balance against this propagation delay, not as an arbitrary limit.

The practical consequence shows up whenever demand exceeds this capacity. Unconfirmed transactions pile up in a waiting area called the mempool, and users compete for the limited space in the next block by attaching higher fees. This is exactly what happens during periods of high demand on Bitcoin or Ethereum, when average fees can spike sharply as users bid against each other for scarce block space. Throughput, in other words, is not just an abstract benchmark, it is the resource that a blockchain's fee market is rationing at all times.

Understanding throughput as a hard, physically grounded limit, rather than a number that can simply be turned up, sets up two important threads for the rest of this section. It explains why scaling a blockchain is a genuinely different engineering problem than scaling a centralized database, and it is the first half of a distinction, throughput versus latency, that is easy to conflate but describes two different user experiences of a blockchain's performance.
